   Companies rebrand themselves for all sorts of reasons. Occasionally it’s a sign of trouble, other times newfound ambition. Some monikers, often following spinoffs or mergers, make us question management’s judgment (looking at you Truist , Mondelez and Abrdn ).

   How do investors know if it’s a bad sign? Research by quantitative analyst Alexander Hübbert shows that companies with a name change not related to a deal underperformed similar ones by more than 5 percentage points on average in the following year.

   But he says that the name change alone means nothing. Basically the entire gap comes from companies that were losing money at the time. They trailed their peers by more than 13 percentage points.

   It’s an interesting result, and it makes sense. A board of directors that’s struggling to fix problems might prefer a cosmetic change to more painful choices.

   What about companies that just want to make people forget about what they do or have done? They’re a mixed bag, and many wouldn’t have been caught by Hübbert’s one-year screen.

   Altria, formerly Philip Morris, is a happy example. It’s still mostly in the controversial business of selling cigarettes. But buying its shares at the time of the 2003 rebrand would have earned an investor nearly 3,000%. That’s more than twice as much as the S&P 500’s total return.

   The most infamous case is probably Enron. A 1986 merger between two boringly-named pipeline companies resulted in an even duller appellation, HNG-InterNorth. Then branding strategists made up an exciting one: Enteron.

   A last-minute check of an encyclopedia revealed that it also means part of the intestine, the thing poop moves through, so the “te” was dropped. After 15 years of heady growth, accounting fraud resulted in what was then the largest-ever U.S. bankruptcy.

   Scandal-plagued Valeant Pharmaceuticals provides a double example. It chose that name to distance itself from earlier troubles when it was ICN Pharmaceuticals. Valeant became a Wall Street darling for years. Then a criminal investigation nearly sank the company.

   Valeant renamed itself Bausch Health in 2018, and some investors saw value in the ashes. Sadly, Bausch has declined by two-thirds since that second name change.

   Hübbert stresses that his signal isn’t useful as a trading strategy. One naming gambit , though, might be close to a sure thing—when companies brazenly ape the theme du jour. There are many examples, with a recent one being woolly sneaker maker Allbirds. 

   It changed its name to NewBird AI in April and its shares surged 580%. Then it became Smartbird in June, sparking another bounce. The only smart thing to do was to sell immediately, The stock is down by 85% since its April jump.

Would a rose by any other name be as profitable?

 

Companies rebrand themselves for all sorts of reasons. Occasionally it’s a sign of trouble, other times newfound ambition. Some monikers, often following spinoffs or mergers, make us question management’s judgment (looking at you Truist, Mondelez and Abrdn).

 

How do investors know if it’s a bad sign? Research by quantitative analyst Alexander Hübbert shows that companies with a name change not related to a deal underperformed similar ones by more than 5 percentage points on average in the following year.

 

But he says that the name change alone means nothing. Basically the entire gap comes from companies that were losing money at the time. They trailed their peers by more than 13 percentage points.

 

It’s an interesting result, and it makes sense. A board of directors that’s struggling to fix problems might prefer a cosmetic change to more painful choices.

 

What about companies that just want to make people forget about what they do or have done? They’re a mixed bag, and many wouldn’t have been caught by Hübbert’s one-year screen.

 

Altria, formerly Philip Morris, is a happy example. It’s still mostly in the controversial business of selling cigarettes. But buying its shares at the time of the 2003 rebrand would have earned an investor nearly 3,000%. That’s more than twice as much as the S&P 500’s total return.

 

The most infamous case is probably Enron. A 1986 merger between two boringly-named pipeline companies resulted in an even duller appellation, HNG-InterNorth. Then branding strategists made up an exciting one: Enteron.

 

A last-minute check of an encyclopedia revealed that it also means part of the intestine, the thing poop moves through, so the “te” was dropped. After 15 years of heady growth, accounting fraud resulted in what was then the largest-ever U.S. bankruptcy.

 

Scandal-plagued Valeant Pharmaceuticals provides a double example. It chose that name to distance itself from earlier troubles when it was ICN Pharmaceuticals. Valeant became a Wall Street darling for years. Then a criminal investigation nearly sank the company.

 

Valeant renamed itself Bausch Health in 2018, and some investors saw value in the ashes. Sadly, Bausch has declined by two-thirds since that second name change.

 

Hübbert stresses that his signal isn’t useful as a trading strategy. One naming gambit, though, might be close to a sure thing—when companies brazenly ape the theme du jour. There are many examples, with a recent one being woolly sneaker maker Allbirds. 

 

It changed its name to NewBird AI in April and its shares surged 580%. Then it became Smartbird in June, sparking another bounce. The only smart thing to do was to sell immediately, The stock is down by 85% since its April jump.
